doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
title: Vocal albums with David Allyn
summary: Mandel describes how he and the singer chose tunes and budgets for albums such as David Allyn's all-Kern Sure Thing, made about 1957-58.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Before we… I don't get too far ahead of ourselves chronologically although I want to get back to your specific, other films later like, The Sandpiper, and The Americanization of Emily, and The Russians are Coming, but what I wanted to do is talk about some of the vocal albums you did in the late 50s with people like David Allyn and Sinatra and Jo Stafford and Mel Tormé.
I guess first of all maybe…
Like the Sure Thing, and the other one that came out about twenty years after you did it, In the Blue of Evening.
Oh yeah, um-hm. Around the same time I did a Dick Hayme’s album, which was good too.

I just think it’d be interesting to talk about how you collaborate with different singers and the similarities and differences of getting together a vocal album in far as say picking tunes, deciding on keys, deciding on orchestration.
We sit down and decide those things, that’s what we do.
For example with David you were doing an all Jerome Kern album with the Sure Thing.

You know with most of those dates at that time it was what can we afford, how big of an orchestra can I have. We’d mutually agree on the songs and you tried to get the nicest orchestra you could and try and get the best mixer you could and record in the best studios you could. That was really the name of the game.
Yeah, the Sure Thing I think in particular is regarded by a lot of people as the record that David Allyn’s best and most fondly known for and remembered for.
It was a labor of love making it. I think we made it in about 1957, something like that.
Seven or eight, yeah, I guess so.
